title: On the future of ecosystem-oriented fisheries management
content:
Abstract
Ecosystem-based fisheries management (EBFM) and ecosystem approaches to fisheries management (EAFM), collectively here called “ecosystem-oriented fisheries management” developed three decades ago. They have become firmly embedded in fisheries science and have slowly and variably integrated into fisheries management. Early literature focused on definitions, the components linking ecosystem science to management, and how analogues to single-species reference points and integrated ecosystem assessments to relate ecosystem processes and management objectives. The initial decade primarily reflected principles of EAFM, with the focus on ecosystem attributes affecting the management of individual stocks and complexes. The second decade of literature increases the focus on ecosystems, alongside individual stocks and steps towards EBFM. Linking of climate issues emerges during this period, as do spatial aspects of ecosystem dynamics and management of a broader scope of human impacts. In the (current) third decade, the increasing focus on climate change impacts and spatially explicit management is consistent with emphasis on the evolution towards more broad-based ecosystem-based management (EBM) emphasizing how fisheries relate to other cross-sectoral interests. The next decades will likely see greater emphasis on global change impacts affecting the productivity of species and ecosystems, and the integration of these concepts into ecosystemic management of multiple-use sectors. Climate impacts and the attendant increase in non-stationarity of population and ecosystem processes will perhaps rival ending overfishing (under current stationarity assumptions) as the primary focal areas of fisheries management. Mediation of cross-sectoral conflicts will require new and more spatially resolved data, predictions, and policy instruments with the goal of minimizing conflicts and negotiating the distribution of costs and benefits accruing to the various sectoral interests. Given all of these simultaneous and, in some cases, conflicting management objectives, undoubtedly the future of ecosystem-oriented fisheries management lies not only within the domain of fisheries but in the broader balancing of ecosystem, social, and economic objectives affecting the oceans. Increasingly, the success of fisheries management will be viewed as critically dependent on also addressing social aspects of fisheries, including community well-being, stakeholder involvement (in both management and science), equitable allocation of costs and benefits, and transparency and credibility of management processes.
